The Registrar’s decision will be subject to any orders made by the court/tribunal."}],"answer":"## Decisions appealable to a court

**The Manual’s account of the statutory appeal routes** identifies the Federal Court and the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) as the relevant courts. It lists these Registrar decisions:

- Rejection of an application, or acceptance subject to conditions or limitations — **s 35**.
- Registration or refusal following opposition, including registration subject to conditions or limitations — **s 56**.
- Decisions on requests to amend an application or another document — **s 67**.
- Decisions on requests to amend registered particulars — **s 83(2)**; amendments for consistency with international agreements — **s 83A(8)**.
- Revocation of registration under s 84A — **s 84D**.
- Opposition concerning removal for non-use — **s 104**. [1–4]

For international marks, the Manual identifies opposition to extension of protection under **reg 17A.34P**, and opposition to cessation of protection for non-use under **reg 17A.48X**. It also lists regs **17A.26 and 17A.42F** as court-appeal provisions, but the supplied passages do not fully explain their scope. [2, 4]

**Regulations supplied directly:** reg 17A.34P applies s 56 to the relevant IRDA opposition decision, substituting the holder for the applicant and the decision under reg 17A.34N for the decision under s 55. The other Act appeal provisions above are described by the Manual; their legislative text has not been supplied, so this is not a complete verification of their scope or who may appeal. [5]

## If there is no appeal right

**Manual account:** first distinguish absence of a court appeal from absence of any statutory review route. The Manual identifies ART review for refusal of an extension of time under s 224(7), and for specified decisions dismissing an opposition because its statement of grounds and particulars is inadequate or deleting material from that statement. [9–10]

If the Act specifies neither a court appeal nor ART review, the Manual says the alternative avenue is **judicial review under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977**. A “person aggrieved” may seek that review in either of the courts above. This is **not a merits rehearing**: it concerns matters such as compliance with legislative procedures, procedural fairness and whether evidence was available to support the decision. The AD(JR) Act itself is not supplied, so its precise eligibility requirements and available remedies cannot be verified here. [6–8]

## Procedure and effect

**Manual account/practice:** a statutory court appeal is described as a de novo re-decision, unlike AD(JR) judicial review. The Manual states a **21-day appeal period**, subject to further time allowed by the court. In its opposition guidance, it says implementation of the Registrar’s decision pauses once an appeal or review is filed, pending determination or discontinuance and subject to court or tribunal orders. [11–13]"}
